newsitem.title: USA: Roche obesity drug seen recommended.
newsitem.headline: Roche obesity drug seen recommended.

text.p: A new anti-obesity drug from Hoffmann-La Roche Inc, a U.S. unit of Switzerland's Roche Holding Ltd, is expected to receive a recommendation for approval from a U.S. Food and Drug Advisory panel meeting on Wednesday, analysts said.
The drug, Xenical, inihibits gastric and pancreatic lipases, or enzymes that play a key role in absorbing dietary fat, in order to treat obesity, the company said.

"The chances for recommendation for approval are very good," Arvind Desai, an analyst at Mehta and Isaly. Because the FDA expedited its review of Xenical, he said he thought the drug would receive final approval by the end of 1997.

Ira Loss, an analyst at HSBC James Capel's Washington Analysis unit, said: "There's a very good chance the FDA will recommend approval of Xenical. This is the first drug for obesity that was submitted with two years of data. Other drugs had only one year, and the data was scanty at that."

Roche said the multi-center, placebo-controlled Phase III trials involved nearly 5,000 obese patients and studied the efficacy of Xenical when taken in conjunction with a mildly hypocaloric diet having one-third of the calories from fat.

It was evaluated in two-year clinical trials for weight loss, maintenance of lost weight and improvement in factors like hypertension, dyslipidemia, impaired glucose tolerance and hyperinsulinemia, the company said.
If Xenical received approval, it could ultimately but not immediately become a big drug for the company, analysts said.

"It would not be catastrophic for Roche if the drug is not recommended for approval, but Xenical could become a sleeper that turns into a big drug for them," Loss said. Desai forecast Xenical sales of about $500 million by its fifth-year on the market, assuming sales started at the end of 1997.
As opposed to other obesity drugs like Interneuron Pharmaceuticals Inc's Redux and BASF AG's Meridia, Xenical acted in the gastrointestinal system rather than the brain, analysts said.

"The primary side effect of Xenical is diarrhea," Loss said. By contrast, Redux was associated with pulmonary hypertension and Meridia was linked to higher blood pressure and cholesterol levels, he said.
"This leaves a big opening for Xenical," he said.
Desai said: "Its side effects are generally more benign."
Hoffman said side effects were generally mild and temporary and were frequently seen among patients who did not follow the appropriate diet regime.
Roche would likely direct its attention toward the more high-risk obesity market, caused by diabetes and heart disease and would then turn to the mass market, Desai said.
"We will have more details after the FDA advisory meeting regarding Phase III data, dosing, side effects and the company's plans," he said.
